headline: Disruptive Raises $10B to Fund 'At Least 10' Companies
subheadline: A mega-fund with the conviction of a dartboard and the thesis of a hedge fund's reject pile.
source_headline: Disruptive raises $10B to make big bets on at least 10 companies
body_html:
Disruptive has closed a $10 billion fund, and in a stunning display of strategic clarity, the firm has committed to making "big bets" on "at least 10 companies." Let that math settle in: ten billion dollars, minimum ten companies, which means each portfolio company can expect an average of one billion dollars—give or take several billion, depending on whether Disruptive decides eight companies is sufficiently close to the original promise. This is what happens when a venture firm gets so much capital that specificity becomes optional, and "at least" becomes a legitimate investment strategy.

Disruptive's recent track record offers a masterclass in conviction-free capital deployment. The firm has poured money into chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs—two industries so flooded with venture capital that the barrier to entry is less about innovation and more about having a compelling deck and a plausible claim that your technology is "doing AI differently." Both companies operate in markets where the largest technology firms on Earth are actively competing, and where commodity capital has effectively replaced differentiation. Yet here is Disruptive, raising another $10 billion to "make big bets," as if checking boxes in an industry checklist qualifies as portfolio construction.

The phrase "at least 10 companies" is doing tremendous work here. It suggests that Disruptive's investors—who presumably handed over ten billion dollars—could not negotiate a firm commitment on the basic parameters of how their money would be deployed. An "at least" in venture capital is the written equivalent of a shrug: maybe it's ten, maybe it's seven, maybe we'll discover some other founder with good connections and drop half a billion on them in Q4. It is the opposite of thesis-driven investing; it is capital-driven allocation dressed up in the language of conviction.

In the press release theater that surrounds every mega-fund announcement, Disruptive will surely invoke language about "disruptive technologies," "secular trends," and "long-term value creation." Translation: we have a lot of money, the limited partners are not asking hard questions, and we need to put it somewhere before someone notices that neither Groq nor ElevenLabs has demonstrated durable competitive advantages or clear paths to profitability. The firm's willingness to say "at least 10" rather than committing to a specific portfolio size suggests that even Disruptive's own leadership is uncertain about what problem it is solving.

History offers scant comfort for mega-fund investors betting this broadly. Softbank's Vision Fund raised $100 billion and proceeded to throw money at office space companies, retail automation, and a litany of startups that have either collapsed or underperformed massively. Benchmark's mega-funds struggled to deploy capital effectively precisely because capital without conviction scales poorly. The firms that have generated genuine returns—Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins in their prime, Accel—succeeded because they had theses, networks, and the discipline to say no. Disruptive is waving a $10 billion checkbook and saying "at least 10," which is the opposite of discipline.

What this deal ultimately reveals about the state of venture capital in 2024 is grim: there is more capital chasing deals than there are genuinely differentiated investment opportunities, and the response has been to raise ever-larger funds with ever-vaguer mandates. Limited partners, desperate for returns and believing that scale itself creates edge, keep writing checks. GPs, drowning in capital they cannot meaningfully deploy with any rigor, respond by widening their nets and lowering their bars. A $10 billion fund betting on "at least 10" companies is not investment strategy; it is capital arbitrage pretending to be venture capital.

When this fund returns disappointing multiples in seven years—because most of its companies will either fail or achieve modest exits in crowded markets—Disruptive will have already raised the next mega-fund, and the cycle will continue. That is the actual disruption here: the disruption of coherent capital allocation.
glossary_definition: Venture capital's way of saying 'we raised too much money and haven't thought this through.'
